cues.text: Now let's understand subnetting instead of memorising a table blindly.
In slash P notation, P counts the network bits.
The mask is a continuous run of ones followed by zeros.
For IPv4, subtract P from thirty-two to find the host bits.
Raise two to that power to find the total number of addresses.
Normally subtract two for the network and broadcast addresses.
Slash thirty-one point-to-point links and slash thirty-two host routes are exceptions.
To find the network address, perform a bitwise AND between address and mask.
Set all host bits to one for the broadcast address.
The table in the notes shows a pattern.
At slash twenty-four, the mask is two fifty-five dot two fifty-five dot two fifty-five dot zero.
There are two hundred and fifty-six addresses and two hundred and fifty-four ordinary usable addresses.
Every time the prefix increases by one, total capacity halves.
Slash twenty-five ends in one twenty-eight: one hundred and twenty-eight addresses, one hundred and twenty-six usable.
Slash twenty-six ends in one ninety-two: sixty-four and sixty-two.
Slash twenty-seven ends in two twenty-four: thirty-two and thirty.
Slash twenty-eight ends in two forty: sixteen and fourteen.
Slash twenty-nine ends in two forty-eight: eight and six.
Slash thirty ends in two fifty-two: four and two.
In every row the first three mask octets remain two fifty-five.
Use the visual table to check the exact masks.
